idiom_name: val properties, data class copy() and immutable collection factories
implementation_notes: The data modifier generates copy(), which constructs a new instance with the named properties replaced - the natural query shape for a model value - and val prevents rebinding of the reference. Both are shallow: the data-class documentation shows a MutableList property whose contents are shared between an instance and its copy, so use read-only types (listOf, toList, immutable fields) for anything inside the value. The standard List/Map/Set interfaces are read-only views over possibly mutable implementations, so a toList() copy is still needed when handing data across an API boundary. Keep vars and mutable collections inside identity-bearing entities and expose their transitions as named commands.
pitfalls: copy() is shallow and val is read-only, not immutable: a MutableList property is shared between an instance and its copy and can be changed through either reference.
Java interop can mutate a Kotlin List - the read-only interface does not stop Java code from casting to MutableList - so copy at boundaries you do not control.
A property with a custom getter can compute or read external state on every access: an impure query hiding behind val.
